Admiral OS uses Bluetooth Low Energy for out-of-box device setup and, once a device is claimed, for cloud-authorised field service (§4.11). The dashboard's Provision over Bluetooth and Repair over Bluetooth pages implement this protocol in the browser. This page covers the full provisioning protocol — advertising, GATT service and characteristic definitions, the provisioning state machine, security model, error codes, and implementation notes for both firmware and mobile clients.

A workload can report its own application metrics, such as a count of robot falls or a battery level, and Admiral charts them next to the system telemetry. The workload writes StatsD-style lines to a local unix socket. The device agent aggregates them and sends them to the same telemetry pipeline as CPU, memory and disk metrics, with the same device and fleet labels.

Set up a new device's network and claim it into a fleet straight from your browser, over Bluetooth. No keyboard, monitor, or companion app is needed on site; this is the quickest way to bring up headless robots, gateways, and devices mounted out of reach.

Admiral OS uses Bluetooth Low Energy for out-of-box device setup and, once a device is claimed, for cloud-authorised field service (§4.11). The dashboard's Provision over Bluetooth and Repair over Bluetooth pages implement this protocol in the browser. This page covers the full provisioning protocol — advertising, GATT service and characteristic definitions, the provisioning state machine, security model, error codes, and implementation notes for both firmware and mobile clients. Open for setup, sealed after claim An unclaimed device accepts any setup session (protected by an on-screen pairing code on devices with a display). Once a device is claimed it no longer accepts open sessions: every capability requires a short-lived, session-bound access token issued by Admiral Cloud and verified on the device, offline (§4.11). A claimed device that has not received verification keys from the cloud does not advertise at all.

The provisioning protocol allows a mobile companion app to: Discover one or more unconfigured Admiral devices in proximity. Identify a specific physical device via LED and on-screen pairing animation. Configure Wi-Fi and/or Ethernet credentials (individually or in batch across 10+ devices). Monitor multi-interface network connection status in real time. Retrieve a cloud-issued pairing key for account association. Read device metadata (firmware version, serial number, hardware revision).

Principle Description Sealed After Claim Open setup is available only while unclaimed. After the claim, access needs a cloud-issued token bound to the session (§4.11). Factory reset returns the device to open setup. Multi-device Batching A mobile app can discover 10+ devices, push the same Wi-Fi config to all of them, and asynchronously harvest their pairing keys. Stateless Mobile The mobile app does not persist BLE connection state. Admiral devices are the source of truth. Minimal MTU Payloads fit within a 512-byte ATT MTU, falling back to 23-byte MTU with chunked transfers if needed. Secure Link All sensitive data (Wi-Fi passwords, pairing keys) is protected via application-layer X25519 ECDH key exchange and AES-GCM encryption.

Admiral devices advertise over BLE only when unprovisioned or when an error occurs before final setup completes. Mode When Active Interval Connectable Notes Setup Factory reset / first boot / no Wi-Fi config 100 ms Yes Enters power-save after 30 min; wakes on button press. With TimeoutMode enabled, drops advertisement after 1 min with no peers or 5 min of connection inactivity. Configuring Wi-Fi credentials received, device connecting 200 ms Yes Continues advertising state changes. Error Wi-Fi connected but cloud unreachable, etc. 150 ms Yes Allows mobile app to reconnect and correct the network config. Service Claimed, holding cloud verification keys On Yes Field service only; every session must authenticate with an access token (§4.11). Off if service mode is disabled or no keys have been received.

MAC Address: To avoid duplicate OUI collisions common in bulk generic microcontrollers, the device overrides the controller's primary physical MAC on boot with a Locally Administered Address (LAA) starting with 0x0A. The remaining 5 bytes are populated from a SHA-256 fingerprint of the true hardware serial number. Offset Length Type Field Value 0 3 0x01 Flags 0x06 (LE General Discoverable) 3 4 0x03 16-bit Service UUID 0xFDA0 7 14 0xFF Manufacturer Data See §2.3 21 12 0x08 Short Local Name UTF-8 (e.g., ADM-QWERT123) UUID Short Form The advertisement broadcasts the 16-bit short UUID 0xFDA0. The full 128-bit GATT service UUID is A0FD0001-C2E1-4F9C-8D2A-0B6C3E4D5F60 — 0xFDA0 is the little-endian byte-reversed form of the A0FD prefix. Mobile clients must use the full 128-bit UUID when discovering and connecting to GATT characteristics.

Byte 0: Protocol Version — 0x01 Byte 1: Device Type — 0x01 (Standard), 0x02 (Pro) Byte 2: Provisioning State — See §2.4 Byte 3: Capability Flags — Bitmask (Bit 3: LED, Bit 4: Display Framebuffer) Byte 4–7: Device ID Hash — Last 4 bytes of SHA-256(hardware serial number) Byte 8: Reserved — 0x00 The 2-byte Company Identifier is transmitted as a separate BLE Manufacturer Data header field and is not included in the 9-byte payload above.

Value State Description 0x00 UNPROVISIONED Ready for setup. BLE active. 0x01 WIFI_CONFIGURED Credentials received, attempting to connect. 0x02 WIFI_CONNECTED Connected to Wi-Fi. Resolving cloud connection. 0x03 CLOUD_PAIRED Pairing key received from cloud, waiting for mobile confirmation. 0x04 FULLY_PROVISIONED Mobile confirmed registration. BLE advertising shuts down. 0xFF ERROR Setup failed. Check Error characteristic (§4.10).

The provisioning lifecycle ensures the device can safely traverse from unconfigured to cloud-paired without getting stuck. Organic Connections: The Admiral OS runs a background daemon monitoring active network interfaces. If an Ethernet cable is attached, or a previously saved Wi-Fi network reconnects organically during the setup loop, the device asynchronously advances to WIFI_CONNECTED (0x02) and then CLOUD_PAIRED (0x03), pushing notifications to the mobile app. The mobile app must listen for state notifications and dynamically skip the Wi-Fi configuration UI if the device is already online.

From To Trigger UNPROVISIONED WIFI_CONFIGURED Mobile writes Wi-Fi credentials via Network Config characteristic UNPROVISIONED WIFI_CONNECTED Organic Ethernet or saved Wi-Fi connects WIFI_CONFIGURED WIFI_CONNECTED Successful Wi-Fi authentication and DHCP lease WIFI_CONNECTED CLOUD_PAIRED Admiral Cloud issues ephemeral pairing key CLOUD_PAIRED FULLY_PROVISIONED Mobile writes COMPLETE to Prov Control characteristic Any ERROR (0xFF) Authentication failure, DHCP timeout, cloud unreachable FULLY_PROVISIONED UNPROVISIONED Physical factory reset (10-second pinhole button hold)

Physical Factory Reset: Holding the pinhole reset button for 10 seconds clears all saved configurations (Wi-Fi credentials under /admrl/conf/, custom local settings). The device rolls back to UNPROVISIONED and restarts BLE advertising on next boot. Setup Mode Recovery: If pairing is aborted or fails before full provisioning, the system remains in or reverts to setup mode and re-initializes the setup-mode BLE advertisement automatically.

Accepts a chunked, application-layer encrypted JSON payload containing network credentials or configuration actions. Chunking​ Payloads must be fragmented into 128-byte chunks with a ~30 ms delay between writes: [Chunk Index (uint8, 0-based)] [Total Chunks (uint8)] [Payload Fragment…] Reassembled payload (minimum 28 bytes): [Nonce (12 bytes)] [AES-GCM Ciphertext + 16-byte Auth Tag] Session Key Exchange​ Mobile reads the device's ephemeral X25519 public key from A0FD0050. Mobile derives the shared AES-256 secret via ECDH and transmits its own public key via the PROV_CTRL START command (A0FD0040) to open the crypto session. Mobile encrypts the JSON payload with AES-GCM and pushes the chunked blob. Payload Actions​ Payloads require an "action" key: save — Push or update a network configuration. { "action": "save", "priority": 100, "type": "wifi", "ssid": "MyNetwork", "psk": "password", "ip": "192.168.1.50/24", "gateway": "192.168.1.1", "dns": "8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1" } Set "type": "ethernet" to skip Wi-Fi authentication and apply settings directly to the Ethernet adapter. Transmitting "psk": "" on an update preserves the existing stored passphrase while merging other fields. Static ip fields must use CIDR notation (e.g., 192.168.1.50/24). Bare IP addresses without a prefix length are rejected by the client before transmission. delete — Remove a saved network profile. { "action": "delete", "ssid": "MyNetwork" } reset — Wipe all Wi-Fi networks and reset Ethernet to DHCP. { "action": "reset" }

Returns the active network state across all concurrent live interfaces. Proactively notifies the client when an organic connection (Ethernet or saved Wi-Fi) is detected, allowing the mobile app to bypass the Wi-Fi setup step. Format: [Interface Count (uint8)] followed by per-interface records: [Link Type (uint8)] [IPv4 Address (4 bytes)] [RSSI (1 byte)] [Label Length (uint8)] [Label (UTF-8)] Link Type 0x02 = hardwired Ethernet. Other values represent Wi-Fi. If fully disconnected, the interface list is empty: [0x00]. SD-WAN failover events (gateway priority shifts from L4 health checks) update this characteristic and push a notification automatically.

Returns paginated results after a SCAN_WIFI command, triggered page-by-page with GET_WIFI_PAGE. Header: [Page Number (uint8)] [List Count (uint8)] Per network record (repeated List Count times): [SSID Length (uint8)] [SSID (UTF-8)] [RSSI (int8)] [Security (uint8: 0x00=Open, 0x02=Encrypted)]

Returns the cloud pairing key sealed with the established session secret. Format: [Nonce (12 bytes)] [AES-GCM Ciphertext + 16-byte Auth Tag] The Device State characteristic (§4.3) transitions Cloud State to 0x04 (Key Ready) when the key is available. The mobile client decrypts it using the existing session secret. Pairing key validity is tied to the device's installation lifecycle, not a time-based TTL. The key is invalidated immediately upon successful cloud account association to prevent replay attacks.

Controls the session lifecycle. Byte(s) Field Values 0 Control Action 0x01 START · 0x02 COMPLETE · 0x03 ABORT 1–32 Mobile Public Key 32-byte X25519 public key (on START only) START (0x01): Transmits the mobile's X25519 public key and opens the encrypted session. Must be called before writing to any encrypted characteristic (Network Config). Establishing the session immediately on initialization also ensures the device can encrypt and push the Cloud Pairing Key even if it connects organically via Ethernet and skips the Wi-Fi setup. COMPLETE (0x02): Signals successful account registration. Triggers immediate shutdown of the BLE stack. ABORT (0x03): Tears down the active session. The device remains in or reverts to setup mode.
Notified on failure. See §6 for the full error code table.

A claimed device stays reachable over Bluetooth for field service, but only to someone the Admiral Cloud has authorised. Authorisation works while the device is offline. Open and service modes. 0052 returns JSON: {"v":2,"mode":"open|service","did":"<device uuid>","nonce":"<b64url>","confirm":true,"verified":false,"busy":false} nonce: 16 random bytes (base64url, no padding), fresh at each START. It is single use: any authentication attempt, good or bad, consumes it. confirm (open mode): the device has a display and requires the on-screen pairing code. verified: the current session has confirmed it. busy (service mode): another authenticated session is live, so a START from a different client will be refused. open: the device is not claimed. Anyone in range may provision it, exactly as in §3. The pairing key is delivered. service: the device is claimed. A session does nothing until it presents a valid access token. The pairing key is never sent, and network details are not published to an unauthorised session. Getting access. The console connects, reads 0050 and 0052, and starts a session (PROV_CTRL START, §4.9). Starting a session issues a fresh nonce; read 0052 again. The console asks the cloud for a token for that device, sending the nonce and the session's public key. The cloud checks the signed-in user's permission on the device and signs a token for five minutes. The console writes the token, encrypted and chunked, to 0080. The device verifies the signature with public keys it received when it last connected to the cloud, so no network is needed. What a token binds. The device ID, the session's public key and the nonce. A captured token is useless on any other connection, and the nonce is single use. Tokens carry scopes, which the device enforces. Scopes are not hierarchical. Scope Grants diag Identify, hardware info, device info, workload status, diagnostics. network Wi-Fi scan and saved networks, Ethernet and IP configuration, network changes. operate Workload control and diagnostics mode, on-device screen control. admin Power (reboot and power off), setup completion, unpair. Scopes follow the user's strongest permission on the device: Device permission Scopes Viewer diag Editor diag, operate, network Admin diag, operate, network, admin Tokens are valid for five minutes by default (15 minutes at most). Service requests. After authentication the console sends encrypted requests to 0081 and receives encrypted responses on 0082. Request and response frames are tagged so a captured message cannot be replayed in the other direction, and each request carries a counter that must increase. Wi-Fi and Ethernet management uses the existing characteristics (0011, 0020), which now require the network scope on a claimed device. One session at a time. While an authenticated session is live, a different client's START is refused and the owner is left untouched. A session is live for 30 seconds after its last request; the console sends a session.ping every 10 seconds to keep a quiet session, and a disconnect frees the device immediately, so a dropped link never locks anyone out. On a claimed device ABORT is ignored, because a write cannot be attributed to a connection and would let any client end the owner's session. Pairing code (unclaimed devices with a screen). The key exchange on an unclaimed device is unauthenticated, so a device with a screen defends against a relay in range: it shows an 8 digit code derived from both public keys and the shared secret, and holds back the pairing key, network details and every command until the user types that code into the console and the console sends it in PROV_CTRL command 0x04 (VERIFY). The console first checks the typed code against its own derivation and sends nothing on a mismatch, because a relay has different keys on each side. The device ends the session after three wrong codes. Devices without a screen keep the open flow. Writing off to /admrl/conf/ble-verify disables the code for fleets that provision with an app that cannot send VERIFY. Rotation and revocation. The cloud sends the device its current set of verification keys on every connection. Removing a key removes its tokens' validity from the fleet on next check-in. Five failed authentications in a row lock authentication on the device for 60 seconds; this counter is device-wide, not per client. Turning it off. Writing off to /admrl/conf/ble-service-mode stops a claimed device advertising at all.

Admiral devices feature an LED and an integrated display. When the mobile app writes the IDENTIFY command (0x01) to A0FD0011: The BLE daemon parses the requested duration (default: 10 seconds). The system LED switches to an active pulsing pattern. The device updates the system display, entering an active Pairing Animation (such as a pulsing connection ring, animated PIN, or avatar). After the specified duration, the LED and display revert to their default states. This ensures a user in a room with multiple identical Admiral devices can identify exactly which unit they are configuring.

Delivered via the Error Info characteristic (A0FD00F0). Domain Code Category Description Resolution 0x11 0x11 Wi-Fi SSID Not Found Trigger a new scan and prompt the user. 0x11 0x12 Network Configuration / Payload Error Check credential payload formatting or valid IP ranges. 0x11 0x13 Network DHCP Timeout Connected to network but failed to obtain IP. Verify the backend router. 0x11 0x14 Wi-Fi Authentication Failed Password rejected by access point. Prompt user to re-enter. 0x11 0x15 Network Delete Network Failed Verify the target SSID matches stored profiles. 0x11 0x16 Network Reset Network Failed OS failed to safely clear previous configuration state. 0x21 0x21 Cloud Unreachable Verify the network has internet access and retry. 0x21 0x22 Cloud Key Generation Failed Admiral Cloud backend failure. 0x30 0x30 System Display Error System could not render to display.

Parameter Value Description Max Concurrent BLE Clients 1 Admiral device accepts only one BLE central at a time. Setup Timeout (No Peers) 60 s With TimeoutMode enabled, drops advertisement after 1 min with no peer connections. Setup Timeout (With Peers) 5 min Drops advertisement after 5 min of connection inactivity. Connection Idle Timeout 30 s Device disconnects if no writes occur within 30 seconds. Wi-Fi Scan Timeout 5 s Scan results must be returned within 5 seconds. Identify Default Duration 10 s LED/splash sequence duration if not explicitly specified.

Admiral OS uses a multi-tiered power-save supervisor to balance discoverability with radio-silence best practices: Unconnected Idle (1 min): If no peer connection is formed within 1 minute while TimeoutMode is active, the supervisor shuts down BLE advertising and sets advertising: false in system state. Connected Inactivity (5 min): If a client connects to the GATT server but commits no writes (commands or config payloads) for 5 continuous minutes, the supervisor disconnects the link, tears down the advertiser, and enters a low-power quiet state. Activity Reset: Any standard activity — new central connection, payload chunk write, identify command — resets the supervisor countdown to zero.

BLE OS-level bonding is bypassed in favor of application-layer encryption to avoid cross-platform bonding complexities. The Admiral device generates an ephemeral X25519 keypair on boot and exposes its public key on A0FD0050. The mobile app generates its own ephemeral keypair, derives the AES-256 shared secret via ECDH, and transmits its public key strictly via the PROV_CTRL START command. This ordering prevents crypto-deadlocks on organic network connections. Subsequent encrypted payloads (Wi-Fi credentials) omit public keys entirely — they are sealed with AES-GCM using the negotiated secret only. Wi-Fi credentials are never readable back to the mobile app over BLE.

An unclaimed device accepts any session so that a fresh device can be set up with no prior trust. Once a device is claimed it is sealed: pairing is closed, the pairing key is never sent again, and every capability needs a cloud-issued, session-bound token that the device validates offline (§4.11). A fault on the device cannot reopen it. A device that has not received verification keys from the cloud does not advertise after it is claimed, as before. A session that was already open when the claim happened stays open until it disconnects, so the setup flow can finish. Resetting the device to factory state (the pinhole button, §3) returns it to the open, unclaimed mode.

For deployments with many Admiral devices in the same space: Mobile app scans for ~10 seconds, accumulating unique Device IDs from advertisement packets. User selects multiple target devices in the mobile app. Mobile app provisions devices sequentially: connect → write Wi-Fi config → disconnect → next device. Devices connect to Wi-Fi and the Admiral Cloud in parallel asynchronously. Mobile app round-robins reconnections to read the Pairing Key from each device as they become ready. Mobile app sends a single batch API request to the Admiral Cloud with all collected keys. Mobile app round-robins reconnections to send PROVISIONING_COMPLETE to all devices, triggering their BLE shutdown. tip Do not hold a BLE connection open while a device is working through a long Wi-Fi connection phase. Disconnect, move to the next device, and return. Holding connections blocks the single-client limit unnecessarily.

Monitor provisioning state on startup. Only enable the HCI interface if provisioning_status != FULLY_PROVISIONED. The IDENTIFY command should trigger the device's physical identity indicators. MAC Address Override: Before initiating any Bluetooth services, open a raw HCI management socket (AF_BLUETOOTH, BTPROTO_HCI) to issue the physical controller address override, enforcing unique LAAs across hardware variants. GATT Cache Purging on Disconnect: To mitigate the iOS Bluetooth GATT service caching bug (where iOS fails to discover updated characteristics on reconnect), remove the device from the system's active device registry and momentarily cycle the advertiser. This forces iOS to prune its GATT service cache.

iOS: Use CBCentralManager. Android: Use BluetoothAdapter.getDefaultAdapter().getBluetoothLeScanner(). Filter scans on Service UUID 0xFDA0. Subscribe to Device State (A0FD0010) and Network Status (A0FD0021) notifications immediately after connecting — both can fire before the UI has progressed past the discovery screen, particularly when Ethernet is already plugged in. Always send PROV_CTRL START with the mobile's X25519 public key before writing to any encrypted characteristic.

Endianness: Little-endian for all multi-byte integers. Strings / JSON: UTF-8 encoded. Chunking: Large payloads (such as chunked command responses) use application-layer chunking to work around the BLE GATT 512-byte hard limit and OS driver-level packet queue limits. Maximum fragment size: 128 bytes. Enforce a ~30 ms delay between chunk writes. Byte 0: Chunk Index (0-based) Byte 1: Total Chunks Byte 2…: Payload Fragment

A workload can report its own application metrics, such as a count of robot falls or a battery level, and Admiral charts them next to the system telemetry. The workload writes StatsD-style lines to a local unix socket. The device agent aggregates them and sends them to the same telemetry pipeline as CPU, memory and disk metrics, with the same device and fleet labels.

Custom metrics are off by default and are not billed. Open the fleet in the dashboard and go to Settings > Custom metrics. Turn on the switch on the Custom metrics card. Devices open the metrics socket as soon as they receive the change. The socket directory is mounted into the workload container when the container is next created, so restart or redeploy the workload (or let the next configuration rollout recreate it) before it can write. Turning the setting off closes the socket on the device; the mount is removed the next time the container is recreated. Changing the setting needs permission to update the fleet.

Item Value Socket path in the container /run/admrl/metrics/metrics.sock Environment variable ADMRL_METRICS_SOCKET (set to the path above) Socket type unix datagram (SOCK_DGRAM) Use the environment variable rather than hard-coding the path. The socket is writable by any user in the container, so the workload does not need to run as root. If the file does not exist, the setting is off for the fleet or the container has not been recreated since it was enabled; treat that as "metrics unavailable" and carry on.

Each datagram holds one or more lines separated by \n: name:value|type name:value|type|#tag1:value1,tag2:value2 Type Meaning c Counter. Each line adds value to a running total. g Gauge. The last value written wins. Examples: robot.fall:1|c robot.fall:1|c|#site:warehouse3,model:r2 battery.level:87.5|g|#slot:0 Malformed lines are dropped.

Tags become labels on the series. These tag names are dropped because they are used by the platform to keep data separated per organisation, fleet and device: org_id, device_id, fleet_id, device, job, instance, __name__, and anything starting with __.

Limit Value Datagram size 8 KiB Distinct series per device 500 Tags per line 8 Metric name length 128 characters Tag value length 128 characters Lines or new series over a limit are dropped. The agent counts them in edge_custom_dropped_total{reason}. Keep tag values low-cardinality (a site name, not a request id), since every distinct tag combination is a separate series.

The agent turns the name into a Prometheus series name: dots and dashes become _, and the result is prefixed with edge_custom_. You write Series Type robot.fall:1|c edge_custom_robot_fall_total counter battery.level:87|g edge_custom_battery_level gauge Counters get a _total suffix. The dashboard lists the series that reported in the last day and shows them with a best-effort name (robot.fall). Because dots and underscores both map to _, the dashboard cannot always recover the original spelling. Charts are in the Custom tab of the fleet's and each device's Telemetry page. On a fleet, counters are charted as the sum of the increase per interval across all devices, and gauges as a median with a p5 to p95 band and the worst device. Both also get a Top devices chart. On a device, each metric gets a plain chart. To query series yourself, use the Query tab on the telemetry page, for example sum(increase(edge_custom_robot_fall_total[1h])).

import os import socket SOCK = os.environ.get("ADMRL_METRICS_SOCKET", "/run/admrl/metrics/metrics.sock") _sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) _sock.setblocking(False) def emit(line: str) -> None: try: _sock.sendto(line.encode(), SOCK) except OSError: pass # metrics disabled or the agent is not listening; never break the app # A robot fall, tagged with the site it happened at emit("robot.fall:1|c|#site:warehouse3") emit("battery.level:87.5|g")

package main import ( "net" "os" ) func main() { path := os.Getenv("ADMRL_METRICS_SOCKET") if path == "" { path = "/run/admrl/metrics/metrics.sock" } conn, err := net.Dial("unixgram", path) if err != nil { return // metrics disabled; carry on } defer conn.Close() conn.Write([]byte("robot.fall:1|c|#site:warehouse3\nbattery.level:87.5|g")) }

With socat: printf 'robot.fall:1|c|#site:warehouse3' | socat - UNIX-SENDTO:"$ADMRL_METRICS_SOCKET" With a netcat that supports unix datagram sockets (nc -uU): printf 'robot.fall:1|c' | nc -uU -w1 "$ADMRL_METRICS_SOCKET"

Enable custom metrics on the fleet and recreate the workload. In the robot software, call emit("robot.fall:1|c|#site:warehouse3") each time a fall is detected. Open the fleet's Custom metrics page and pick robot.fall (counter). The first chart shows falls per interval across the fleet, and Top devices shows which robots fall most.

The socket does not exist in the container. Check that the setting is on and that the container was recreated after enabling it. Nothing appears in the dashboard. Allow a minute or two for the first values, and make sure the time range covers the writes. A datagram over 8 KiB or a malformed line is dropped without an error to the workload. Some series are missing. The device may be over its 500-series limit; check edge_custom_dropped_total in the Query tab.

Set up a new device's network and claim it into a fleet straight from your browser, over Bluetooth. No keyboard, monitor, or companion app is needed on site; this is the quickest way to bring up headless robots, gateways, and devices mounted out of reach. Open Devices > Provision over Bluetooth (https://app.admrl.co/devices/provision). The Add Host dialog also links here (Device not set up yet? Provision it over Bluetooth).

Browser: Chrome or Edge on desktop, or Chrome on Android. Safari and Firefox do not support Web Bluetooth; the page tells you if your browser cannot be used and offers Add host with a pairing key instead. Proximity: your computer or phone within Bluetooth range of the device. Device: an unclaimed Admiral device (new, or factory reset). It advertises as ADM-XXXXX.
The wizard runs through Connect, Network, Pair and claim, and Finish. A collapsible Activity log shows every step as it happens.

Click Find device and choose the device (ADM-XXXXX) in the browser's device chooser. If the device is already claimed, the wizard says so and offers Repair this device over Bluetooth, which opens Bluetooth Field Service.

A device with a display shows an 8-digit pairing code. Type it into the browser and click Confirm code. The browser checks the code itself before sending anything, which proves you are connected to the device in front of you and not to an impostor nearby. Three wrong codes end the session. Headless devices skip this step.
documents.s: 2. Confirm the Pairing Code (devices with a screen)

documents.t: A summary card shows the device's model, firmware, displays, and setup state. Click Identify to make the device beep if you have several in front of you. If the device is already online (for example on wired Ethernet), choose Continue with this connection. Wi-Fi: pick a scanned network (signal strength and security are shown) or Enter a network name manually. Saved networks can be forgotten from the list. Leave the password blank to keep a saved one. Ethernet: DHCP by default. Both tabs offer Use a static IP address (address in CIDR form, gateway, DNS) and Use an HTTP proxy. Click Connect and continue. Joining a network can take up to a minute.

The device sends its pairing key over the encrypted Bluetooth session and the dashboard validates it. Enter a Device name, choose a Fleet, and optionally set a latitude and longitude. Click Claim device.
The wizard waits for the device to check in to Admiral Cloud, completes setup, and disconnects Bluetooth. Choose Open device, Finish now, or Provision another device.

Every Bluetooth session is end-to-end encrypted at the application layer with a fresh key exchange; Wi-Fi passwords are never readable back over Bluetooth. The 8-digit pairing code defends devices with a screen against relay attacks during setup. Once a device is claimed, it no longer accepts open setup sessions. Only users authorised in Admiral Cloud can open a field service session. For the full protocol, see BLE Provisioning Protocol.

Pairing (claiming) adds a device to your Admiral organisation and assigns it to a fleet. There are three ways to do it: Method Best for Pairing key (this page) A device with a screen that is already online. Type the key from its screen into the dashboard. Bluetooth provisioning Headless devices, or devices that need Wi-Fi set up first. Done from your browser. Auto-provisioning Batches and factory flashing. Devices claim themselves on first boot.

When Admiral Base OS boots for the first time or after a factory reset, the on-device console shows the device's pairing key, a short code of 5 to 8 characters. On the new on-device console, a QR code is shown next to the key. Scanning it opens the Add Host page with the pairing key already filled in and validated. If you are not signed in, you are taken to the sign-in page first and returned to the same page afterwards. Case-Insensitive Encoding (No Ambiguous Characters) Pairing keys use the digits 2 to 9 and the letters A to Z except I, L, and O, so nothing can be confused with 0, 1, or each other. Keys are case-insensitive and do not expire, so hardware can be staged and claimed later without racing a timer. Key characteristics: Character set: Case-insensitive, 5 to 8 characters, from 2-9 and A-Z without I, L, and O. Non-expiring: Keys stay valid until the device is claimed. Identity: Bound to the device's unique hardware UUID. Pairing key vs. pairing code The pairing key claims the device into your organisation. The 8-digit pairing code is different: it appears only during Bluetooth provisioning and confirms that your browser is talking to the device in front of you.

Log in to the Admiral Dashboard. Navigate to Devices > Add Host (or click Add Host inside any fleet). Enter the pairing key displayed on your device. The dashboard validates it as you type. Provide a descriptive name (e.g., AMR-Warehouse-04 or Sydney-Kiosk-01). Assign the device to a Fleet. (Optional) Provide geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude). Click Add Device. The device pairs with your organisation, connects to the Admiral Mesh, and appears in your fleet's device list.
documents.s: Adding the Device in the Dashboard

documents.t: Once claimed, the device moves straight into its operational lifecycle: Admiral Mesh connection: Connects to the Admiral Mesh with a credential scoped to its own identity and renewed daily. A device can never see another device's traffic. Configuration sync: Fetches the fleet's workload configuration and any secret files. Network sync: Applies the fleet's Wi-Fi networks in priority order. Image pull: Pulls the container image into a dedicated Copy-on-Write (CoW) subvolume. Hardware access: Passes through the /dev tree (motor controllers, SocketCAN, cameras, LiDAR, GPU accelerators) before starting the workload. Telemetry: Begins sending metrics, logs, and security posture to Admiral Cloud. A claimed device stops accepting open Bluetooth setup sessions. From then on, only users authorised in Admiral Cloud can connect to it over Bluetooth, through Field Service.

Check for typos. The dashboard normalises input to uppercase and filters out disallowed characters. Make sure the device has outbound network access. If the console shows Can't connect to Admiral, press F3 on a connected keyboard (or tap Wi-Fi in the bar at the bottom of a touch screen) to open the Wi-Fi screen, or use Bluetooth provisioning to set up the network from your browser.

Verify outbound network access. The Admiral Mesh automatically falls back from TCP to UDP and then to WebSocket over HTTPS port 443 to stay connected over restrictive or high-latency links. Run diagnostics on the device's screen (F2), or over Bluetooth from Field Service.

This page takes a new organisation from nothing to a device running a container. The dashboard's setup guide does most of it for you; the same steps are listed below if you would rather do them by hand. It finishes with an example container you can use to confirm everything works before you bring your own software.

The dashboard setup guide (https://app.admrl.co/get-started) covers everything in four steps. New organisations are taken there automatically the first time an owner, admin, or member opens the dashboard. Each step unlocks once the previous one is done. Progress is worked out from what already exists in your organisation, so you can leave and come back at any time; Skip setup closes the guide.

A configuration describes the workload your devices run: its container image, environment, volumes, and hardware access. Select an existing configuration, or click Create configuration to open the configuration editor. No container yet? Use the example container. Click Continue.

A fleet groups devices that run the same configuration. Enter a name (and optionally a description and location) and click Create fleet and continue. The fleet is created with the configuration from step 1 already assigned. To use a fleet you already have instead, pick it under Or use a fleet you already have and click Use this fleet; it is switched to the chosen configuration.

A provisioning profile produces installer images that join devices to your fleet on first boot without manual pairing. Accept the suggested name (<fleet> installer) or change it, add optional tags, and click Create profile and continue.

Choose the architecture, board, and image type, then download. See Download Options. Write the image to a USB drive or SD card (Installation covers flashing), boot your device from it, and it appears in your fleet. The page shows Waiting for your first device... and updates when devices connect. Click Finish when you are done, or I will do this later.

Until the guide is finished, the dashboard home page shows a Finish setting up card with your next step and progress. Continue setup returns to the guide; Dismiss shrinks it to a reminder strip with Reopen setup guide. The card disappears once the guide is complete or any device has joined. The Devices, Fleets, and Configurations pages also show Start setup guide (or Continue with the next step) while they are empty.

Install Admiral OS. Download the Admiral Base OS image for your hardware (x86_64 or ARM64), write it to the target media, and boot the device. See Installation. Pair the device. Pairing (claiming) adds the booted device to your organisation. Type the key from the device's screen into the dashboard (Pairing), set up a headless device from your browser (Bluetooth Provisioning), or flash a pre-enrolled image that claims itself on first boot (Auto-Provisioning). Create a fleet. Open Fleets, create one, and assign your paired device to it. Deploy a workload. Open Configurations, create one, and assign it to your fleet. The device pulls the image and starts it.

If you do not have a container ready, use the Admiral demo container. Source github.com/AdmrlOS/admrl-demo Image ghcr.io/admrlos/admrl-demo/systemd-container:main Architectures amd64 and arm64 In the configuration editor, paste the image name into Workload Image. In the dashboard, Use example container in the create-configuration dialog fills it in for you.

The image is built from the repository's Dockerfile: Based on Ubuntu 26.04, with systemd as the container's init process (CMD ["/lib/systemd/systemd"], stop signal SIGRTMIN+3). It is a system container, not a single-process one. Installs the Ubuntu minimal GNOME desktop, with GDM set to log a user in automatically and Wayland enabled, plus Mesa graphics drivers (and the Intel media driver on amd64) so it can render on the device's display. Adds an OpenSSH server and basic network tools (iproute2, ethtool, kmod). Masks services that would conflict with the host (NetworkManager, snapd, the full udev trigger, text-mode login) and limits udev triggering to display, graphics and input hardware. Installs Google Chrome on amd64 only; Google does not publish an arm64 build. Use it on hardware with a display and a GPU to see a full desktop session started by Admiral. It is a demo for trying out the platform and is not intended for production use. Source and issues are in the repository.
Roll changes out safely with Rollouts. Watch your devices in Device Operations & Monitoring.
